# 2020 Jonesboro tornado

## Lead section

The 2020 Jonesboro tornado was a significant meteorological event that occurred on March 28, 2020, in Jonesboro, Arkansas. This powerful tornado, rated EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale with maximum winds of approximately 140 mph, caused extensive damage to the city's southern and eastern sections, destroying or damaging more than 200 homes and businesses . Despite its severity, the tornado resulted in no fatalities, though it injured 22 people . The tornado's impact was notably influenced by the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, which had reduced the number of people in public spaces like the Mall at Turtle Creek .

This tornado was the strongest to hit Arkansas since April 27, 2014, and the most powerful to strike Jonesboro since 1997 . Governor Asa Hutchinson declared a state disaster in response to the damage, which officials estimated at "several hundred million dollars" . The event is often cited as a "warning success story" due to the ten-minute advance warning that allowed residents to seek shelter .

## Meteorological synopsis

The 2020 Jonesboro tornado developed from a supercell thunderstorm that formed as part of a larger severe weather outbreak affecting much of the central United States on March 28, 2020 . The storm's intensity was fueled by record-warm temperatures for that time of year, with the Little Rock National Weather Service Office noting that "a warm front exited to the north of the state, and ushered in well-above-average temperatures in the 80s to lower 90s" .

The same supercell that produced the Jonesboro tornado also spawned another tornado near Amagon, Arkansas, with winds estimated at 110 mph and a path just over five miles long . Weather offices around the area measured wind gusts up to 74 mph, strong enough to derail a nearby train and injure 20 people .

The National Weather Service's damage survey determined that the Jonesboro tornado touched down just north of Interstate Highway 555, initially producing EF-2 damage at the Mall at Turtle Creek before strengthening to EF-3 force as it moved through the Jonesboro Municipal Airport and beyond . At its widest point, the tornado left a swath of damage one-third of a mile across, along a path of more than twelve miles .

## Event timeline

The sequence of events on March 28, 2020, began with the issuance of Tornado Watch #68 for the Jonesboro area approximately two hours before the tornado struck . The National Weather Service issued the tornado warning at 4:47 p.m. CDT, and the tornado touched down just ten minutes later at 4:57 p.m. CDT .

Eyewitness accounts and video footage captured the tornado's destructive path through the city. One resident recorded video from inside his phone shop showing the massive tornado tossing debris around . The tornado struck at roughly 5:20 p.m. local time, according to initial reports, and prompted an immediate search and rescue operation .

The timing of the tornado—late Saturday afternoon—was significant. Emergency management officials noted that "at 5 o'clock on a Saturday afternoon that place would've been packed, and at this point there was hardly anyone in there," referring to the Mall at Turtle Creek . This reduced foot traffic was attributed to COVID-19 restrictions that had closed many businesses and encouraged social distancing .

## Impact and damage

The 2020 Jonesboro tornado caused widespread devastation across approximately 13 miles of southern and eastern Jonesboro . The tornado heavily damaged or destroyed more than 200 homes and businesses, with 55 homes completely destroyed and requiring total rebuilding .

The most notable commercial casualties included the Mall at Turtle Creek and the Jonesboro Municipal Airport . At the Mall at Turtle Creek, extensive damage occurred with most stores closed due to the coronavirus pandemic . A Best Buy store at the mall was rendered "nearly unrecognizable" by the tornado's force . The shopping center's damage was so severe that the property later sold for redevelopment, as the original lender was "unwilling to reconstruct and carry the loan" .

The Jonesboro Municipal Airport suffered catastrophic damage, with the tornado destroying the terminal building and numerous hangars . Two airplanes at the airport required heavy machinery to move after being tossed by the tornado's winds . The Federal Emergency Management Agency later approved $5 million in federal funding to build a new airport terminal, which will be matched with $1.3 million in local funds .

Other significant damage occurred at industrial and commercial properties. Camfil, located at 3505 Airport Road, received a direct hit from the tornado, though the factory was searched and cleared with no reported injuries . Power outages affected sections of the city, and wreckage tossed by the tornado blocked roads, complicating emergency response efforts .

The tornado's path of destruction also claimed the home of Dr. Jared Burks, a physician who had been living apart from his wife Alyssa and their son Zeke while treating COVID-19 patients during the pandemic . Though their home was completely destroyed, all three family members survived and later set up a GoFundMe page for assistance .

## Aftermath and recovery

Following the tornado, Governor Asa Hutchinson immediately declared a state disaster in the Jonesboro area and requested federal assistance to rebuild the affected communities . The governor stated, "I want to assure all of Jonesboro and northeast Arkansas that the entire state has been in prayer. I have not seen this kind of devastation from a tornado since I have been governor" .

Emergency response efforts were coordinated through multiple agencies and organizations. The American Red Cross and Salvation Army established staging areas to plan cleanup and relief operations . The Arkansas Army National Guard's 875th Engineer Battalion delivered 200 cots to assist with shelter operations, arriving just after midnight on March 29 .

The city of Jonesboro established four emergency shelters for displaced residents, including University Heights, Fox Meadow and Nettleton Steam Schools, as well as Journey Church on Disciple Drive . Mayor Harold Perrin initially issued a 7 p.m. curfew, though other sources report a 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew from Sunday night into Monday morning .

Damage assessment efforts were complicated by immediate cleanup efforts that began shortly after the tornado, making it difficult for officials to conduct comprehensive surveys . The Red Cross reported being approximately 35 percent complete with damage assessment within days of the event .

The financial impact was substantial, with officials estimating total damage costs at "several hundred million dollars" . Governor Hutchinson noted that all businesses destroyed by the tornado qualified for COVID-19 disaster loans, providing additional support during the recovery process .

Community support and charitable donations poured in to aid recovery efforts. Regions Bank announced a \$10,000 contribution to the Jonesboro tornado recovery fund established by United Way of Northeast Arkansas . Arvest Bank partnered with the United Way to assist those affected by the tornado . Operation BBQ Relief, with the help of Dewayne and Q49 Smokehouse, provided 1,700 meals over two days to first responders and impacted residents .

Long-term recovery has shown significant progress. By May 2022, approximately 40 percent of homes destroyed in the tornado were occupied by new owners . The city launched its first-ever housing division dedicated to securing new housing, working with organizations involved in tornado recovery to determine outstanding needs .

The Jonesboro Municipal Airport's reconstruction is underway with the $5 million federal grant approved by the Economic Development Administration, an agency within the U.S. Department of Commerce <reference type="end" id=29>. The airport commission is contributing an additional $1.3 million in funding to replace the terminal and hangars destroyed in the tornado .

## Notable aspects

The 2020 Jonesboro tornado is particularly notable for several reasons. First, it was the first major weather disaster to occur during the COVID-19 pandemic shutdown era in the United States . The pandemic's influence on the tornado's impact cannot be overstated—reduced foot traffic in public spaces likely prevented numerous fatalities .

The tornado is also significant for its meteorological characteristics. It was the strongest tornado to hit Arkansas since April 27, 2014, and the most powerful to strike Jonesboro since 1997 when an F-3 tornado (on the old Fujita Scale) affected the city .

Emergency management officials have highlighted the tornado as a "warning success story" due to the ten-minute advance warning provided by the National Weather Service . The warning, issued at 4:47 p.m. CDT, gave residents sufficient time to seek shelter before the tornado touched down at 4:57 p.m. CDT .

The tornado's timing—late Saturday afternoon during the COVID-19 pandemic—created unique circumstances. The Mall at Turtle Creek, which suffered extensive damage, was largely empty due to pandemic restrictions, which emergency officials described as a "blessing in disguise" . Similarly, the Jonesboro Municipal Airport, while damaged, had reduced activity due to travel restrictions.

## Conclusion

The 2020 Jonesboro tornado stands as a significant event in Arkansas's meteorological and social history. This EF3 tornado, with its 140 mph winds and twelve-mile path of destruction, demonstrated both the destructive power of severe weather and the effectiveness of modern warning systems . The fact that no fatalities occurred despite the tornado's strength and the densely populated areas it affected is attributed to excellent warnings and the coincidental timing during the COVID-19 pandemic .

The tornado's impact on Jonesboro's infrastructure—including the destruction of the Mall at Turtle Creek and Jonesboro Municipal Airport—has necessitated substantial rebuilding efforts . The city's response, including the establishment of emergency shelters, coordination with state and federal agencies, and community support through charitable donations, exemplifies effective disaster management .

Looking forward, the recovery efforts continue to reshape Jonesboro's landscape. The construction of a new airport terminal, the redevelopment of the mall site, and the rebuilding of residential areas demonstrate the community's resilience . The 2020 Jonesboro tornado serves as a reminder of the importance of preparedness, early warning systems, and community support in the face of natural disasters.

Two tornadoes in May were assigned ratings of EFU (unknown) because there was no damage to evaluate. The latest tornado (rated EF1) affected areas near Romance (White County) on November 15th. The strongest tornado (rated EF3/maximum winds around 140 mph) tracked just under 13 miles through the south/east side of Jonesboro (Craighead County) on March 28th. This was the strongest tornado in the state since April 27, 2014. ![Image 5: In 2020, above average temperatures (in red) occurred in six months, and above average precipitation (in green) was noted in nine months. Overall, it was a little warmer and a lot wetter than normal.](https://www.weather.gov/images/lzk/cmsimgs/trendst2020.jpg) Temperature Trends|Precipitation Trends In the picture: In 2020, above average temperatures (in red) occurred in six months, and above average precipitation (in green) was noted in nine months. Overall, it was a little warmer and a lot wetter than normal. Looking statewide, this was the third year in a row with precipitation more than ten inches above average. It was the 11th wettest year dating back to 1895. At least four tropical systems contributed to the soggy scenario (Cristobal in June, Laura in August, Beta in September, and Delta in October). The year began with very mild and wet conditions from January through March. In six of seven months to follow. temperatures were below average and precipitation was above average. The reset button was hit in November, with precipitation shutting off (very dry), and temperatures warming up (very mild). The Black, Cache, Ouachita, and lower White Rivers were high to overflowing at times through the spring. Fields were either under water or too wet for use through much of the beginning of the growing season. The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) released a report on August 12th, and it was mentioned that the state had 1.1 million unplanted (or prevented) acres. JONESBORO ARKANSAS TORNADO 2020: A WARNING SUCCESS STORY
========================================================

![Image 7: tornado in sky](https://midlandusa.com/cdn/shop/articles/1daf482d2ba735a10d06889e2cde584c_aabd7eb2-ab14-4c8f-9c36-7585ed539fc2.jpg?v=1746477120&width=1800)

Table of Contents
-----------------

*   [No Fatalities Reported](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story#no-fatalities-reported)
*   [Tracking the Tornado](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story#tracking-the-tornado)
*   [Early Warning Was Key](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story#early-warning-was-key)

A Tornado Warning Success Story
===============================

On Saturday, March 28, 2020, ten minutes after the National Weather Service issued its warning, a strong tornado with top winds estimated at 140mph, plowed a twelve mile long path through portions of Jonesboro, AR.The Jonesboro Arkansas Tornado in 2020 damaged or destroyed more than 200 homes and businesses, including Turtle Creek Mall and the city airport.

No Fatalities Reported
----------------------

Eighteen people were injured, but amazingly, no one was killed. Isolation due to the COVID-19 coronavirus meant the mall and other businesses were much less crowded than they would have been on a typical Saturday afternoon. Most importantly, the tornado warning was issued at 4:47 pm and the twister touched down at 4:57pm, meaning those ten minutes allowed everyone plenty of time to seek shelter and survive.

Tracking the Tornado
--------------------

The National Weather Service damage survey found that the twister touched down just north of Interstate highway 555, produced EF-2 damage at the Mall, then strengthened to EF-3 force as it destroyed buildings and airplanes at the Jonesboro Airport and beyond. At its widest, the funnel left a swath of damage one-third of a mile across, along a path of more than twelve miles.

Early Warning Was Key
---------------------

Occurring on a March day (the middle of Arkansas’ tornado season), just before 5pm (the most common time of day for Arkansas tornadoes), and two hours after Tornado Watch #68 had been issued for the area, the tornado was not unexpected, meaning the people of Jonesboro were well aware of the day’s severe weather risk. Warnings from the National Weather Service via weather radio and cell phone, combined with outstanding on-air coverage by local television and radio stations undoubtedly saved lives. As the 2020 tornado season kicks in, everyone can learn a good lesson from the Jonesboro tornado: know your risk for severe weather, have multiple redundant methods of receiving warnings, watch your local TV station’s storm coverage, and have a practiced, well-understood plan of action to get to your safe place.

Every home, school, and business should have a [Midland NOAA Weather Alert Radio](https://midlandusa.com/collections/weather). As the official “Voice of the National Weather Service”, it keeps you informed and alerted no matter what you’re doing. Buy it, plug it in, and be prepared.

40 percent of homes destroyed in March 2020 tornado now occupied by new owners

by Jackie DelPilar 

Thursday, May 12th 2022

![Image 6: A pile of rubble including wood planks and personal items sit in the middle of a neighborhood](https://fox17.com/resources/media/68ff6be8-477c-4eec-93a7-09c30189e619-large16x9_tornado.jpg?1652406122937)

The March 2020 tornadoes killed 19 people in Putnam County and injured 87 others. (Photo: WZTV)

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WZTV) —

Sam and Tina brown were sleeping in their North Nashville home when the March 2020 tornado jolted them out of bed.

ADVERTISEMENT

“We tried to make it out of the house but a tree fell on the house so we end up getting stuck in there,” Tina said.

Read More

After about 40 minutes under debris, the Browns finally made it out from the rubble, shaken, but physically ok.

As the Browns and their neighbors sifted through their belongings, the couple says investors approached them in droves, encouraging them to sell.

“They come offer you like $100,000, $150,000. We can't live off $150,000. Can't rebuild off of that,” Sam said.

And it wasn’t just North Nashville.

Neighbors in the hardest-hit areas of East Nashville say they also experienced the investor invasion.

“It was troubling, right after the storm because you're literally standing in the middle of rubble. And people are talking to you and you're like, do you see what's going on, you know, have a little feeling,” neighbor Tom Larson said. Larson is one of the few remaining neighbors on Holly Street, the most densely impacted area in the city.

Some neighbors stood firm and found a way a rebuild.

But others are long gone.

FOX 17 News dug through city data to find out how many homes that were demolished have been sold to new owners. We used planning department records to learn which homes were demolished, then checked property sales for those units.

City property data shows about 40 percent of all homes destroyed in the March 2020 tornado currently have new owners.

Some of the properties have changed hands two or more times in the past two years.

Records show more than a dozen different development companies were involved in the sales.

Non-profit leaders say it's commonplace for investors to approach homeowners after disasters.

And while it may be frowned upon, it’s all perfectly legal.

“It didn't take some would call the vultures, some would call savvy businesspeople, or opportunists to begin,” Dr. Paulette Coleman said.

Coleman volunteered with Lee Chapel in North Nashville immediately after the storm. She also sits on the affordable housing task force with the nonprofit Nashville Organized for Action and Hope (NOAH).

She says many North Nashville homeowners didn’t have insurance, making those investor deals that much more enticing.

“We discovered that even those who were homeowners and maybe had generation or heir property, were not insured. And if they were insured, they were not adequately insured, given the escalation of land value,” Coleman said.

Nonprofit leaders say both homeowners and renters displaced by the storm struggled to find a new place to live in the city within their budget, making the housing market even more challenging.

FOX 17 News reached out to Mayor John Cooper’s office to find out what’s being done to help tornado victims, and others in need of affordable housing.

A spokesperson with the planning department sent a statement, saying since the tornado, Metro launched its first-ever housing division dedicated to securing new housing.

They are working with organizations involved in tornado recovery to determine outstanding needs.

One of those organizations is the Equity Alliance. They went door to door after the tornado to inform homeowners of their options through the “Don’t sell out Norf” campaign.

“This is where the residents live, it's where they work, it's where they play, it's where they thrive. So if we're displacing them, then where do they go? What do they do,” Equity Alliance Communications Director Tereva Parham said.

Some families, like the Browns, took that information to heart.

They rebuilt thanks to donations from a local church and help from family.

“We weren't going nowhere, we stuck like chuck, this is our house this is our home, and couldn’t nobody buy it,” Sam said.

But for others displaced by the tornado, living in Nashville has become a distant memory.

Non-profit leaders say around 80 percent of the homes impacted in North Nashville were being rented.

The city doesn’t keep track of renters as they come and go, so we will never know the true impact of renters getting displaced.

The full statement from the Planning Department is listed below:

1.What has been the tornado's impact on housing? As you know, the Housing Division had not yet been created when the tornado devastated parts of Nashville. The Housing Team has been in contact with the organizations that played key roles in tornado recovery to determine outstanding housing needs. Please contact the Community Foundation for specific information.

2.Any affordable housing efforts underway? Metro’s first-ever Housing Division was launched at the beginning of this year at the recommendation of the Mayor’s Affordable Housing Task Force. In just a few short months, the Housing Division has worked on securing the most investment in the history of the Barnes Fund, building the City’s capacity to address Nashville’s housing needs by developing a scope for a unified housing strategy and creating new tools and policies.

For example:

a.Unified Housing Strategy: Align systems across responsive Metro departments, agencies, partners and resources. Goal is to kickoff late Summer 2022.

b.Catalyst Fund: A new fund, seeded initially with $20 million in ARP funding, to preserve affordable housing and allows affordable housing developers to compete against market rate developers. Metro is issuing an RFP in the coming weeks to bring on a third-party fund manager to manage the program.

c.Mixed Income PILOT: Passed by Council on May 5, this provides tax abatements to create affordability in market-rate developments that would not otherwise offer affordable options. Expected to create 300 units annually.

d.Participation Agreements: Up to $4 million to be used for enhanced public infrastructure improvements (i.e., sidewalks, streetlights, etc.) related to affordable housing development. First $2 million to be made available by the end of May.

3.What can be done to ease some of the housing cost burdens many Nashvillians are experiencing? While creating and preserving affordable housing is vital in our community, it’s also important to ensure housing security for all. That may mean to keep someone in their current, desired housing to connect them with resources that can lead to a job with better wages, employment closer to home to cut down on transportation costs, access to affordable childcare near home or work, etc.

It also looks like empowering our residents with the knowledge and tools to navigate housing resources and understand the complexity of housing challenges.

Later this summer, we plan to build out a resident portal utilizing $200,000 in ARP funds to connect residents to housing opportunities.

We believe that to understand the needs in our community it’s vital to regularly engage with residents, council members, community groups and others to create a person-centric and neighborhood appropriate solutions.

Jonesboro, Arkansas (Tornado) / 1,700 Meals Over 2 Days
=======================================================

March 29, 2020

![Image 10: Jonesboro, Arkansas (Tornado) / 1,700 Meals Over 2 Days](https://obr-wp-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/07094055/ar_jonesboro_2020.jpg)

On the evening of March 28, 2020, a supercell thunderstorm produced several tornadoes in Arkansas. The most significant tornado was an EF3 tornado that ripped through Jonesboro. With winds up to 140 miles per hour, the tornado damaged homes, businesses, and an airport over a 12 mile stretch. This deployment hit close to home because our own Director of Disaster Coordination, Dewayne Daniel, lives in the area. With the help of Dewayne and Q49 Smokehouse, Operation BBQ Relief was proud to provide meals to first responders and impacted residents.

Gov. Hutchinson declares Jonesboro tornado a state disaster

by KATV

Sunday, Mar 29th 2020

![Image 6: Severe roof damage with collapsed shingles and plywood sheeting, framing timbers exposed, and debris scattered around, including insulation, bricks, and a black flexible duct, after a storm](https://katv.com/resources/media/0751e542-703e-4695-940f-c9526ee3e692-large16x9_Burk1.JPG?1585512139341)

![Image 7: Gateway Tire of Arkansas store with collapsed roof and walls after a severe weather event with a white car and a truck parked outside](https://katv.com/resources/media/739914c1-c69a-4af3-8ef3-1139ac9f573d-medium16x9_GATEWAYTIRES.JPG?1585512913090)[![Image 8: A 14x10 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://katv.com/resources/defaults/news_3.0/icons/ui/sbg-gallery_w.svg) 3 View All Photos ![Image 9: Traffic is diverted at an intersection near a building that was destroyed, possibly by a tornado, with power lines overhead and repair crews at work](https://katv.com/resources/media/9b0edb03-2c14-4ff5-b34f-de48a3712c3a-medium16x9_CARAWAY.png?1585524675974)](https://katv.com/news/local/gallery/22-injured-total-2-hospitalized-no-casualties-reported-in-jonesboro-tornado)

The Burks' family, who been living apart while Jared Burks treats patients with COVID-19, has lost their home in a northeast Arkansas tornado. (Photo: ABC)

LITTLE ROCK (KATV) —

Governor Asa Hutchinson declares a state disaster in the Jonesboro area after an EF3 tornado Saturday night and called for federal assistance to rebuild the area.

ADVERTISEMENT

“I want to assure all of Jonesboro and Northeast Arkansas that the entire state has been in prayer. I have not seen this kind of devastation from a tornado since I have been governor," said Hutchinson.

Read More

All of the businesses destroyed by the Jonesboro tornado qualify for COVID-19 disaster loans, according to the governor.

{sd-embed class="sd-embedded-media" data-alt="LSM-3-29-2020-Jonesboro-Arkansas-Tornado-Damage-Major-Damage-to-Homes-Wildwood-Area-Adair-Clement" data-caption="Major%20damage%20to%20homes-%20in%20the%20Wildwood-after%20a%20tornado%20touched%20down%20in%20Jonesboro.%20(Video%20credit:%20Live%20Streams%20Media/%20Adair-Clement)" data-duration="302.86933333333354" data-externalid="b5bd0cf02e4f46449a45f7823200e6ed" data-mediatype="video" data-renditions="" data-thumburl="https://sinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com/b5bd0cf02e4f46449a45f7823200e6ed/thumbnails/poster.jpg" data-title="Major%20damage%20to%20homes-%20in%20the%20Wildwood-after%20a%20tornado%20touched%20down%20in%20Jonesboro.%20(Video%20credit:%20Live%20Streams%20Media/%20Adair-Clement)" data-url="https://sinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com/b5bd0cf02e4f46449a45f7823200e6ed/hls/index.m3u8" data-embed-file="%3Cdiv%20class=%22sda-VideoEmbed%22%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%3Ciframe%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20class=%22sd-embeded-player-iframe%20sda-VideoEmbed-iframe%22%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20src=%22/resources/embeds/vod.html?externalId=b5bd0cf02e4f46449a45f7823200e6ed&thumbUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fsinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com%252Fb5bd0cf02e4f46449a45f7823200e6ed%252Fthumbnails%252Fposter.jpg%22%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20frameborder=%22no%22%3E%3C/iframe%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%3Cdiv%20class=%22sda-VideoEmbed-caption%22%3EMajor%20damage%20to%20homes-%20in%20the%20Wildwood-after%20a%20tornado%20touched%20down%20in%20Jonesboro.%20(Video%20credit:%20Live%20Streams%20Media/%20Adair-Clement)%3C/div%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%3C/div%3E" data-embed-type="video" contenteditable="false"}{/sd-embed}

Officials said The Red Cross is about 35 percent complete with assessing tornado damage in Jonesboro. 55 homes were completely destroyed and will need to be rebuilt.

Gov. Hutchinson said the state is waiting to find out if the damage reached the threshold to declare the tornado a federal disaster, to get assistance from FEMA. He believes it does meet the federal requirement for aid

KATV content partner [Region 8 News](https://www.kait8.com/2020/03/28/tornado-warnings-issued-throughout-region-craighead-poinsett-counties-pm/ "https://www.kait8.com/2020/03/28/tornado-warnings-issued-throughout-region-craighead-poinsett-counties-pm/")left 22 injured and two people hospitalized.

16x9%22,%22scaleWidth%22:648,%22url%22:%22/resources/media/739914c1-c69a-4af3-8ef3-1139ac9f573d-medium16x9_GATEWAYTIRES.JPG?1585512913090%22,%22width%22:958,%22x%22:28,%22y%22:0,%22uuid%22:null,%22id%22:%2245c0384d-9fc1-4b77-87f8-2723cb638c3c%22,%22preciseWidth%22:null,%22preciseHeight%22:null,%22name%22:%22medium16x9Url%22,%22rendition%22:%22medium16x9%22,%22labelOrConvertedName%22:%22medium16x9%22%7D%7D" data-embed-type="image" contenteditable="false" }<="" sd-embed="">{/sd-embed}

Officials reportedly said the two people were required to be hospitalized with non-life threatening injuries, and no casualties have been reported.

Crews on Airport Road reported no injuries and only minor gas leaks from a few cars that were thrown upsidedown. Jonesboro Airport has also been searched and cleared.

Two airplanes there will require heavy machinery in order to move. Camfil, located at 3505 Airport Rd., has also been searched and cleared with the factory taking a direct hit, according to Region 8.

{sd-embed class="sd-embedded-media" data-embed-file="%3Ciframe%20src=%22https://www.facebook.com/plugins/video.php?href=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.facebook.com%252FKATVChannel7%252Fvideos%252F258406875170468%252F&show_text=0&width=560%22%20width=%22560%22%20height=%22315%22%20style=%22border:none;overflow:hidden%22%20scrolling=%22no%22%20frameborder=%220%22%20allowTransparency=%22true%22%20allowFullScreen=%22true%22%3E%3C/iframe%3E" data-embed-type="facebook" contenteditable="false"}{/sd-embed}

{sd-embed class="sd-embedded-media" data-embed-file="%3Ciframe%20src=%22https://www.facebook.com/plugins/video.php?href=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.facebook.com%252FKATVChannel7%252Fvideos%252F2318935858400301%252F&show_text=0&width=560%22%20width=%22560%22%20height=%22315%22%20style=%22border:none;overflow:hidden%22%20scrolling=%22no%22%20frameborder=%220%22%20allowTransparency=%22true%22%20allowFullScreen=%22true%22%3E%3C/iframe%3E" data-embed-type="facebook" contenteditable="false"}{/sd-embed}

The family behind [a viral Northeast Arkansas mom's photo](https://katv.com/news/local/the-story-behind-a-viral-photo-of-an-arkansas-doctor-and-his-son "https://katv.com/news/local/the-story-behind-a-viral-photo-of-an-arkansas-doctor-and-his-son") shows that shows her son and husband separated by a glass door, have lost their home in the tornado.

Dr. Jared Burks has been living apart from his wife Alyssa and their son Zeke while he treats patients during the coronavirus pandemic.

Jared, Alyssa and their son Zeke are okay and have set up a go fund me page, to donate, click [here](https://www.gofundme.com/f/1yo5w210mo "https://www.gofundme.com/f/1yo5w210mo").

{sd-embed class="sd-embedded-media" data-alt="U0X54X70KjaLoY22" data-caption="Aerial%20tornado%20damage%20video%20in%20Jonesboro.%20Video:%20Live%20Storms%20Media/Brent%20Adair)%7Bp%7D%7B/p%7D%7Bp%7D%7B/p%7D" data-duration="123.49866666666675" data-externalid="f04b28f7b894407aa91f996585043a31" data-mediatype="video" data-renditions="" data-thumburl="https://sinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com/f04b28f7b894407aa91f996585043a31/thumbnails/poster.jpg" data-title="Aerial%20tornado%20damage%20video%20in%20Jonesboro.%20Video:%20Live%20Storms%20Media/Brent%20Adair)" data-url="https://sinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com/f04b28f7b894407aa91f996585043a31/hls/index.m3u8" data-embed-file="%3Cdiv%20class=%22sda-VideoEmbed%22%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%3Ciframe%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20class=%22sd-embeded-player-iframe%20sda-VideoEmbed-iframe%22%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20src=%22/resources/embeds/vod.html?externalId=f04b28f7b894407aa91f996585043a31&thumbUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fsinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com%252Ff04b28f7b894407aa91f996585043a31%252Fthumbnails%252Fposter.jpg%22%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20frameborder=%22no%22%3E%3C/iframe%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%3Cdiv%20class=%22sda-VideoEmbed-caption%22%3EAerial%20tornado%20damage%20video%20in%20Jonesboro.%20Video:%20Live%20Storms%20Media/Brent%20Adair)%7Bp%7D%7B/p%7D%7Bp%7D%7B/p%7D%3C/div%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%3C/div%3E" data-embed-type="video" contenteditable="false"}{/sd-embed}

The Arkansas Army National Guard delivered 200 cots to assist the city of Jonesboro to facilitate shelter operations after a Saturday's tornado, said the agency in a press release.

The 875th Engineer Battalion delivered the cots just after midnight. The Guard said it stands ready to assist further if officials need help.

The city has set up four shelters for people to use. They include University Heights, Fox Meadow and Nettleton STEAM Schools as well as Journey Church on Disciple Drive in Jonesboro.

{sd-embed class="sd-embedded-media" data-alt="3-29-20%20Mall,%20Airport,%20Train%20Arials%20Source%20KAIT" data-caption="Aerial%20damage%20of%20airport,%20Turtle%20Creek%20Mall,%20and%20train%20deraining%20in%20Jonesboro.%20(Video:%20KAIT8)%7Bp%7D%7B/p%7D" data-duration="84.60000000000005" data-externalid="7581f97caf0f4009a1af5117ac93126b" data-mediatype="video" data-renditions="" data-thumburl="https://sinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com/7581f97caf0f4009a1af5117ac93126b/thumbnails/poster.jpg" data-title="Aerial%20damage%20of%20airport,%20Turtle%20Creek%20Mall,%20and%20train%20deraining%20in%20Jonesboro.%20(Video:%20KAIT8)" data-url="https://sinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com/7581f97caf0f4009a1af5117ac93126b/hls/index.m3u8" data-embed-file="%3Cdiv%20class=%22sda-VideoEmbed%22%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%3Ciframe%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20class=%22sd-embeded-player-iframe%20sda-VideoEmbed-iframe%22%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20src=%22/resources/embeds/vod.html?externalId=7581f97caf0f4009a1af5117ac93126b&thumbUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fsinclair-vod-assets.sinclairstoryline.com%252F7581f97caf0f4009a1af5117ac93126b%252Fthumbnails%252Fposter.jpg%22%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20frameborder=%22no%22%3E%3C/iframe%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%3Cdiv%20class=%22sda-VideoEmbed-caption%22%3EAerial%20damage%20of%20airport,%20Turtle%20Creek%20Mall,%20and%20train%20deraining%20in%20Jonesboro.%20(Video:%20KAIT8)%7Bp%7D%7B/p%7D%3C/div%3E%0A%20%20%20%20%3C/div%3E" data-embed-type="video" contenteditable="false"}{/sd-embed}

Officials say their best estimate for damage costs: “several hundred million dollars."

[Boozman Welcomes $5 Million Federal Investment at Jonesboro Airport](https://www.boozman.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/press-releases?ID=6111C6FA-D6DE-4FE5-9208-E5E806167FF0)
=============================================================================================================================================================================

#### Feb 27 2024

**WASHINGTON–**U.S. Senator John Boozman (R-AR) applauded an announcement from the Economic Development Administration (EDA) that it is awarding a $5 million grant to the city of Jonesboro, Arkansas for airport infrastructure improvements to support job creation and economic development in the region.

The EDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Commerce, is helping fund construction of a new terminal at the Jonesboro Municipal Airport, replacing one destroyed by a tornado in 2020. This investment will be matched with $1.3 million in local funds.

“As the anchor of northeast Arkansas, Jonesboro’s economic contributions are vital. While extensive damage from a tornado in 2020 threatened disruption and uncertainty, the community rallied together to rebuild and revitalize opportunity that this grant will accelerate through rehabilitating and upgrading key travel infrastructure. I’m pleased this investment will further the recovery effort by improving the airport’s functionality and potential for growth, and in turn benefit the entire region,” **Boozman said**.

“This EDA grant will help ensure that Jonesboro Municipal Airport has the infrastructure needed to increase shipping services, expand regional travel, and create more good paying jobs that will transform the local economy,” **said Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo**.

“The Economic Development Administration works closely with local communities to support locally driven disaster recovery and resiliency,”**said Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Economic Development Alejandra Y. Castillo**. “This project will provide critical infrastructure repairs and improvements at the Jonesboro Municipal Airport, creating jobs and diversifying the regional economy.”

This project was made possible by the regional planning efforts led by the East Arkansas Planning and Development District (EAPDD). EDA funds EAPDD to bring together the public and private sectors to create an economic development roadmap to strengthen the regional economy, support private capital investment and create jobs.

 These projects are funded under the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2023, which provided EDA with $483 million in additional Economic Adjustment Assistance (EAA) Program funds for disaster relief and recovery for areas that received a major disaster declaration under the Robert T. Stafford Act as a result of Hurricanes Ian and Fiona, wildfires, flooding, and other natural disasters occurring in calendar years 2021 and 2022.

========================================================================================

 By David Aaro [Fox News](https://www.foxnews.com/)

#### [Severe threat through tonight: Fox weather forecast](https://www.foxnews.com/video/6145528680001)

Chief Meteorologist Rick Reichmuth discusses yesterday's tornados as well as what to expect this week.

A fierce[tornado](https://www.foxnews.com/category/us/disasters/tornado) tearing through [Arkansas](https://www.foxnews.com/category/us/us-regions/midwest/arkansas)on Saturday left six people injured and caused major damage to a local shopping mall and airport.

Extensive damage occurred at the Mall at Turtle Creek in Jonesboro, although most stores were closed due to the [coronavirus](https://www.foxnews.com/category/health/infectious-disease/coronavirus) pandemic. A Best Buy store was rendered nearly unrecognizable.

“At 5 o’clock on a Saturday afternoon that place would've been packed, and at this point there was hardly anyone in there,” Jonesboro E-911 Director Jeff Presley said. “It’s a blessing in disguise.”

![Image 21: placeholder](https://static.foxnews.com/static/v/all/img/clear.gif)

**[MIDWEST BRACES FOR STORMS, TORNADOES AMID CORONAVIRUS, STAY AT HOME ORDERS](http://www.foxnews.com/us/midwest-braces-for-storms-tornados-amid-coronavirus-stay-at-home-orders)**

Those hurt in the college city of roughly 75,000 people-- about 130 miles northeast of Little Rock -- were taken to the hospital with minor injuries, Presley said. The National Weather Service issued tornado warning around 4:47 p.m. local time and the twister touched down just after 5 p.m., per [the Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/weather/2020/03/28/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado/).

Photos of a destroyed hangar and a graveyard of planes were also captured at the Jonesboro Municipal Airport.

Whoops! We couldn't access this Tweet.

One resident recorded video from inside his phone shop of the massive tornado tossing debris around like it was nothing.

Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., described the effects of the twister and called for support for the community.

"In the midst of everything, a tornado just went through the heart of town," Crawford added."None of my staff have been hurt and my family are okay. Unsure of others - please pray for first responders now being dispatched."

**[MISSISSIPPI TORNADO LEVELS DOLLAR GENERAL STORE, DAMAGES OTHER BUILDINGS](http://www.foxnews.com/us/mississippi-tornado-levels-dollar-general-store-damages-other-buildings)**

![Image 22: placeholder](https://static.foxnews.com/static/v/all/img/clear.gif)

A livestream by KAIT-TV in Jonesboro showed extensive damage to some of the city's businesses.Arkansas State University said on Twitter that its campus wasn't damaged.

Power was out in sections of the city and some of the wreckage tossed by the tornado was seen blocking roads.Jonesboro Mayor Harold Perrin issued a 7 p.m. curfew, and authorities asked people not to drive around.

The home of Dr. Jared Burks, who has been living apart from his wife Alyssa and their son Zeke in Northeast Arkansas while he treats patients with COVID-19 was completely destroyed, per Little Rock's KATV-TV. All three family members were safe.

Forecasters with the Storm Prediction Center in Norman, Okla., warned that a severe weather outbreak was possible later Saturday for much of the central U.S.

Jonesboro Mall Site Sells, Redevelopment Plans Take Shape![Image 19: Lock Icon](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/wp-content/themes/wpp-ark-biz-wp/images/key-icon.svg)
======================================================================================================================================================================

by [Griffin Coop](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/author/gcoopabpg-com/ "Posts by Griffin Coop") -  September 22, 2025, 12:00am

*   [](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.arkansasbusiness.com%2Farticle%2Fjonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment%2F&t=Jonesboro+Mall+Site+Sells%2C+Redevelopment+Plans+Take+Shape%26lt%3Bimg+src%3D%5C%26%23039%3B%2Fwp-content%2Fthemes%2Fwpp-ark-biz-wp%2Fimages%2Fkey-icon.svg%5C%26%23039%3B+alt%3D%5C%26%23039%3BLock+Icon%5C%26%23039%3B+class%3D%5C%26%23039%3Block-icon%5C%26%23039%3B%26gt%3B "Share on Facebook")

*   [](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&ro=true&trk=EasySocialShareButtons&title=Jonesboro+Mall+Site+Sells%2C+Redevelopment+Plans+Take+Shape%26lt%3Bimg+src%3D%5C%26%23039%3B%2Fwp-content%2Fthemes%2Fwpp-ark-biz-wp%2Fimages%2Fkey-icon.svg%5C%26%23039%3B+alt%3D%5C%26%23039%3BLock+Icon%5C%26%23039%3B+class%3D%5C%26%23039%3Block-icon%5C%26%23039%3B%26gt%3B&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.arkansasbusiness.com%2Farticle%2Fjonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment%2F "Share on LinkedIn")
*   [](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/# "Share on Email")
*   [](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/# "Share on Print")

 7 min read 

![Image 20: Jonesboro Mayor Harold Copenhaver called the mall site “the missing piece” in Jonesboro’s economic development.[Sarah Guffey]](https://arkansasbusiness.wppcdn.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/AS5A1083_opt-920x615.jpg)

 Jonesboro Mayor Harold Copenhaver called the mall site “the missing piece” in Jonesboro’s economic development. (Sarah Guffey) 

A large, empty area separates Dillard’s and Target at The Mall at Turtle Creek in Jonesboro. The vacant expanse was once under roof, connecting the mall’s anchor stores with a food court and about 100 shops.

But the mall has languished [since a tornado tore through it in 2020](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboros-boom-rides-out-storm/), leaving storefront wreckage and complicated loan and insurance issues in its wake. The retail magnet that once drew excited crowds on its opening day was eventually torn down in 2023, and now surviving stores such as Dillard’s, Target and JC Penney operate on the perimeter of vacant land.

Today, more than five years after the tornado, the mall might finally be ready for a fresh start.

On Sept. 10, the mall property sold in an online auction for $4.85 million to a real estate investor from northeast Arkansas. [Joshua Brown](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/), cofounder of commercial real estate brokerage Haag Brown, represents the buyer and said the plan is to build a 96,000-SF building he described as an “open air power center,” a type of large, outdoor open-air shopping center.

Brown declined to identify the buyer, but a new entity, Turtle Creek Jonesboro LLC, was incorporated two days after the auction, according to Arkansas secretary of state records. That filing lists Keith Bayird of [Paragould](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/) as the incorporator of the business. Bayird owns several auto dealerships and real estate holdings in northeast Arkansas and southeast Missouri.

[![Image 21: Advertisement for Bank OZK, featuring a woman in a business suit using her phone and the text A Greater Business Partner.](https://img.nui.media/banners/media/0/373/0/3831/1706306603868_Digital_Ad_2__300x250_px_px.jpg)](https://abpg.nui.media/pipeline/441/0/cj?ajkey=V1293AC1FAAJ-573J8100I37312222FDE9L711195L724091QJ2123QQP0G00G0L72409121C17E9E000001010000G0PG30H36W87d9038da2DW4e9eb2DW443022DW4a2162DX1208744969d702G0G074)

Reached by phone, Bayird would not confirm he was the purchaser of the mall.

Regardless of who eventually takes ownership of the property, local officials are eager for it to become usable again.

On a recent tour of the site, Jonesboro Mayor Harold Copenhaver hailed a variety of projects happening across Arkansas’ fifth-largest city, including a nearby sports complex that is under construction. But Copenhaver said he knows the value of resurrecting The Mall at Turtle Creek. “This is the missing piece,” he said.

### Opening Day Excitement

On March 29, 2006, The Mall at Turtle Creek opened on Jonesboro’s Highland Drive to great excitement and was one of the last indoor malls built in the United States.

On the day of the grand opening, a report from Jonesboro’s KAIT-TV said some shoppers arrived before sunrise. The mall’s general manager told the station he was speechless at the community’s response to the mall’s opening and that he “never imagined it would be this big.”

Two years before the mall opened, Belz-Burrow Development Group and David Hocker & Associates Inc. announced plans for the $100 million retail development at the intersection of Highland Drive and Stadium Boulevard in Jonesboro. (The city of Jonesboro renamed a portion of Stadium Boulevard to Red Wolf Boulevard in 2013.)

Developer Marty Belz, the head of a large property development company in Memphis, said at the time he expected the mall would draw shoppers from northeast Arkansas and southeast Missouri. He forecast that the new mall would create 1,500 jobs and have an annual estimated retail sales of $225 million.

### Ownership & Performance

Between the mall’s highly anticipated opening and its sale this year, its ownership is a little hard to pin down.

In 2006, the mall was initially owned by Mall at Turtle Creek LLC, which was incorporated by David Hocker & Associates Inc., a mall developer from Kentucky, according to state and local records.

In 2012, Jonesboro-based property developer Bruce Burrow filed for bankruptcy and, two years later, Belz filed for bankruptcy as well.

In 2013, the mall was sold for $88.7 million to RPI Turtle Creek Mall LLC, according to county property records. The new owner was associated with Rouse Properties Inc., a publicly traded real estate investment trust focused on malls. The purchase price included Rouse taking over the mall’s $79.5 million mortgage.

The mall appeared to be in good shape in 2013 with an occupancy rate of 92% and sales at $370 per SF, according to Green Street, a national commercial real estate research and advisory firm. But in the years leading up to the 2020 tornado, the mall’s sales stagnated and the occupancy rate fell to about 85%, a representative of Green Street estimated.

In 2016, Brookfield Asset Management Inc., a New York-based firm with a variety of holdings including real estate, purchased Rouse Properties Inc.

### Loan Tornado

The 2020 tornado did more than damage the mall; it damaged the collateral the owner had used to secure a loan that was sold to investors.

In 2016, Brookfield used the mall to secure a commercial mortgage-backed security, a type of loan that is turned into a security or bond and sold to investors.

According to Fitch Ratings, which evaluates bonds and other securities, Brookfield secured the CMBS loan with 329,328 SF of “in-line space” in the mall. In-line spaces are the storefronts that line the walkways around the inside of a mall.

![Image 22: Turtle Creek Village shopping center featuring Chico's, Barnes and Noble bookstore, Best Buy store, parking lot with cars, sculpture of a girl on a turtle, benches, bushes, and walkways](https://arkansasbusiness.wppcdn.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/turtle-Creek-mall-Clinton-044.jpg)

The Mall at Turtle Creek is seen here before it suffered damage from a tornado in 2020. (File photo)

When the 2020 tornado swept through the mall, it damaged “the majority of the collateral property” for the loan, according to Fitch. Brookfield was “unwilling to reconstruct and carry the loan,” the report from Fitch said. In 2022, the owners “received substantial insurance proceeds,” the rating service said.

The special servicer, a third party that commonly manages CMBS loans, continued work on the site with anchor tenants that were able to operate after the storm. The special servicer would ultimately seek a sale of the site, Fitch said.

That sale appears to have occurred on Sept. 10 when the mall was sold at auction. The auction website noted the mall was being sold “unencumbered by existing debt.”

After the tornado struck, the mall was in a state of limbo with tenants waiting for a chance to get back into their storefronts. Eventually, many of the tenants moved to new spaces around town.

Copenhaver, the Jonesboro mayor, said that, after the tornado, it was difficult for the owners to sort out who had what responsibility for property damage and restoration and that multiple insurance companies were involved.

Spinoso, the management company that operated the mall, had an office on-site, which Copenhaver said was very helpful but eventually that office was closed and the company became “nonresponsive,” he said.

In 2023, Spinoso said it was necessary to demolish the mall to improve its safety and appearance and to prepare the mall for the future.

### Local Ties

Brown is very familiar with the Turtle Creek property and even credits the property with helping launch his business.

Brown graduated from [Arkansas State University](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/) and wrote his college thesis on the tax increment financing district that helped fund the mall site. The mall’s development and its location allowed Brown to coordinate 30 real estate projects over about five years on Red Wolf Boulevard, but that changed when the tornado struck.

“The tornado hit and the spigot turned off on Red Wolf,” Brown said.

Since that time, former mall tenants have relocated to other parts of Jonesboro and he’s noticed other shopping destinations have popped up in other northeast Arkansas towns like [Searcy](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/) and [Batesville](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/).

The sale of the mall and the fact that the unnamed buyer is local are good for the site, according to Brown. “Best-case scenario,” he said.

[Mark Young](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/), president and CEO of the [Jonesboro Regional Chamber of Commerce](https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/jonesboro-mall-site-redevelopment/), said a local owner of the mall will understand the local retail landscape, particularly Jonesboro’s ability to draw visitors from a larger area than many people recognize.

“It’s not just about Jonesboro and our MSA,” he said. “It truly is about northeast Arkansas and southeast Missouri. We pull from a very large area and that’s beneficial to any retailer that’s in our market.”

Several businesses survived the storm and are still in operation at the mall site and on its outparcels. Dillard’s, JC Penney and Target — all of which own their own stores and weren’t part of the sale — are in operation adjacent to the vacant mall space. The outparcels, which were part of the sale, include Chick-fil-A, Chili’s and Chuck E Cheese restaurants.

Copenhaver, Brown and Young each spoke favorably about an amendment that Arkansas state legislators referred to next year’s general election ballot that would allow cities and counties to create economic development districts. The proposal would allow the community to financially support economic development projects, including retail projects like The Mall at Turtle Creek, similar to the way a TIF district would operate.

Regardless of the fate of that amendment, Copenhaver cautioned that construction on the Turtle Creek site is still years away. Brown estimated the deal would close in 60 to 90 days and said construction could reasonably begin in 2026.

Young said the mall has the potential to be a “significant point of pride” for the community and the auction website hailed the mall site as “the most desirable parcel in Jonesboro, Arkansas.”

Brown sees potential for it too. “As the cards sit right now, it looks really good to be able to pull something off there that makes it a regional attraction again,” Brown said.

![Image 36: A light white airplane takes off from a runway](https://talkbusiness.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/airplane23-1.jpg)

The Jonesboro Municipal Airport will receive a $5 million in grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce, U.S. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo said. The grant will be used to build a new airport terminal, after the old one and numerous hangars were destroyed in the March 2020 tornado.

The Airport Commission will add to the grant with $1.3 million in funding, Airport Manager George Jackson said. A time table for building the new terminal was not released.

[![Image 38: Bank Better 1 Block](https://cdn.broadstreetads.com/assets/fe3364ad-3cce-4b80-82d5-e0044538a696.jpg)](https://www.fsbank.com/ "Bank Better 1 Block")

“This EDA grant will help ensure that Jonesboro Municipal Airport has the infrastructure needed to increase shipping services, expand regional travel, and create more good paying jobs that will transform the local economy,” Raimondo said.

Mayor Harold Copenhaver said this fills a need he has talked about with U.S. Senators John Boozman and Tom Cotton, and U.S. Rep. Rick Crawford, since taking the mayor’s office in 2021. He also thanked the East Arkansas Planning and Development District for its work with EDA.

“This is just another commitment from Sens. Boozman and Cotton, and Rep. Crawford to our airport and its significant impact on our community,” Copenhaver said. “With this funding, plus the $5 million that was allocated in a number of grants last year, air travel to and from Jonesboro is going to be much better for decades to come.”

Boozman noted the importance of Jonesboro’s economic contributions as the anchor of Northeast Arkansas, as well as the extensive damage of the tornado that ripped through the heart of the city.

“The community rallied together to rebuild and revitalize the opportunity that this grant will accelerate through rehabilitating and upgrading key travel infrastructure,” Boozman said. “I’m pleased this investment will further the recovery effort by improving the airport’s functionality and potential for growth, and in turn benefit the entire region.”

“This pivotal support will undoubtedly propel our regional growth and enhance the airport’s vital role in Northeast Arkansas,” Jackson said.

The funding comes from the federal Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2023, which provided $483 million in Economic Adjustment Assistance to areas that suffered major disasters in 2021 and 2022.

_**UPDATED 3/29/2020 12:41 p.m.**_:

_**UPDATED 3/29/2020, 11:00 a.m.**:_ The City of Jonesboro confirms 22 people were injured in Saturday's tornado; all minor injuries.

Curfew will be in effect tonight from 9:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. This does not affect those going to work.

[Post](https://www.facebook.com/TheJonesboroPD/posts/534740694101516) by [TheJonesboroPD](https://www.facebook.com/TheJonesboroPD).

**_UPDATED_**: **_3/28/2020_** - A tornado ripped through Jonesboro Saturday afternoon, leaving a lot of destruction in its path.

First responders, along with the American Red Cross and Salvation Army, set up staging to plan clean up and relief efforts.

Mayor of Jonesboro Harold Perrin, along with first responders, are still canvassing neighborhoods to count the number of injuries. Saturday evening officials counted six.

Turtle Creek Mall was hit heavily by the storm. Most of the building was destroyed and what was a Barnes & Noble store and a Best Buy store were unrecognizable. Perrin said he was grateful people were social distancing by not being at the mall because there could have been fatalities or more injuries.

"I think those numbers would have been much higher if the Coronavirus had not been out," Perrin said.

15.title: Picking Up the Pieces—Carefully—after an EF3 Tornado in Arkansas
15.description: Coronavirus-related closures may have saved lives in Jonesboro, but they are also complicating recovery efforts.
15.content:
_**Above:**_ _This photo from the Mall at Turtle Creek in Jonesboro, Arkansas, from Sunday, March 29, 2020, shows severe damage inflicted by a tornado late Saturday, March 28. (_[_Jonesboro Police Department_](https://www.facebook.com/TheJonesboroPD/photos/pcb.534831167425802/534827574092828/?type=3&theater)_via Facebook)_

The first U.S. weather disaster of the coronavirus-shutdown era hit the northeast Arkansas city of Jonesboro on Saturday afternoon. A tornado rated as EF3 by the National Weather Service office in Memphis tore across southern and eastern Jonesboro around 5 pm CDT. Top winds were estimated at 140 mph along a 12.6-mile path.

The Jonesboro tornado emerged from an intense, fast-moving supercell that had already dropped an [EF1 tornado](https://twitter.com/NWSLittleRock/status/1244435167457886209) between the towns of Algoa and Amagon, Arkansas, about 45 minutes earlier.

Damage appears to be widespread, but the human toll from the Jonesboro tornado was remarkably low: only 22 people were injured, with just two of them hospitalized, as [reported](https://weather.com/news/news/2020-03-28-severe-weather-tornado-impacts-plains-south-midwest) by weather.com. The twister developed right over a dense commercial district on what would have normally been a weekend afternoon packed with shoppers and vehicles. Even though the state of Arkansas [has not yet implemented](https://www.kcur.org/post/resisting-calls-stay-home-order-governor-pushes-personal-responsibility#stream/0) a stay-at-home order in response to the coronavirus pandemic, many businesses in Jonesboro were already shuttered, including a mall that suffered major damage.

While the coronavirus shutdown may have saved lives in Jonesboro, it is complicating recovery efforts, as [reported](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/29/us/tornado-coronavirus-arkansas.html) by the New York Times. With social distancing guidelines ruling the day, residents cannot gather as they normally would in churches and community centers for mutual support and information exchange. “You do what you have to do to meet the need at the moment, and right now, this is what we’re doing,” city councilman Bobby Long told the Times. “We’re doing our best to keep the virus under control. We will not abandon those people who need us the most at this time.”

The coronavirus-related shutdown has also thrown monkey wrenches into the clean-up effort after the deadly tornadoes that hit the Nashville area on March 3, [according to](https://www.csmonitor.com/USA/2020/0327/When-tornadoes-are-only-the-first-of-your-worries) the Christian Science Monitor.

**An outbreak that underperformed**
-----------------------------------

Saturday was [expected](https://www.wunderground.com/cat6/serious-tornado-threat-widespread-large-hail-on-tap-for-saturday) to be a busy tornado day—and it was—but, thankfully, it fell short of its potential. As of Monday, the NOAA/NWS Storm Prediction Center had [logged](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/climo/reports/200328_rpts.html) 24 tornado reports for Saturday. Most of these were in Iowa and Illinois, where a fast-moving spring storm and a strong warm front had been expected to serve as focal points for tornado development.

Late-morning thunderstorms left more cloudiness than predicted across northern and central Illinois, which cut down on instability and reduced the extent and strength of the resulting tornadic supercells near the surface low and warm front. The NWS/Quad Cities office was still carrying out storm surveys on Monday, with at least one EF1 [confirmed](https://twitter.com/NWSQuadCities/status/1244346932790726656) near Leon Corners, Illinois. Several short-lived tornadoes in central Iowa were [rated EF0 or EF1](https://twitter.com/NWSDesMoines) by the NWS/Des Moines office, and at least two tornadoes could not be rated because they did not strike any damage indicators (buildings, utility poles, or other objects).

Instability was greater and wind shear was plentiful toward the south, where the day’s strongest tornadoes ended up forming. Along with the EF3 in Jonesboro, a [pair](https://twitter.com/NWSPaducah/status/1244668906817675264) of EF2 tornadoes from a long-lived supercell struck near the Ohio River, one near Henderson, Kentucky, and the other in and near Newburgh, Indiana, just southeast of Evansville. Both tornadoes damaged dozens of homes, [according to](https://www.weather.gov/pah/mar28svere) the NWS/Paducah office.

**A somewhat active tornado season thus far**
---------------------------------------------

The “[inflation-adjusted](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/adj.html)” tornado count of 189 for the year through March 29 is a bit above average, close to the 75th percentile in a long-term database. (The inflation adjustment takes into account the increase in tornado reports in recent decades as more of the weakest tornadoes are caught on camera.)

Without an inflation adjustment, January and February ranked as the [sixth busiest start](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/sotc/tornadoes/202002) to the tornado year in records going back to 1950, with a preliminary total of 117 tornado reports.

![Image 1: Article image](https://s.w-x.co/inflation-adjusted-tornadoes-1.1-3.29.20-930px.jpg)Annual tornado count for 2019 through March 29, together with percentiles from a longer-term database (1954-2007). (NOAA/NWS/SPC)

The tornado death toll for 2020 so far—33—is unusually high for the first three months of the year. Of that total, 25 deaths occurred in the outbreak of March 2-3 that brought deadly tornadoes to Middle Tennessee.

Just as August is too soon to know whether a full hurricane season will be a busy one, we’re only now shifting into the most active three months of tornado season. On average, roughly half of U.S. tornadoes occur from April through June.

Slight-risk areas were in place by midday Monday for both Monday and Tuesday. Severe storms may track across northern and western Texas and western Oklahoma [on Monday afternoon and evening](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/outlook/archive/2020/day1otlk_20200330_1630.html). The setup suggests a low tornado threat but a chance of very large hail. A somewhat greater severe threat, including tornadoes, may evolve [on Tuesday](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/outlook/archive/2020/day2otlk_20200330_1730.html) as the severe weather shifts into southern Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia and the Florida Panhandle. See weather.com for a [frequently updated outlook.](https://weather.com/storms/severe/news/2020-03-28-severe-thunderstorms-heavy-rain-flooding-south-early-week)
